- **Diagnosis:** **venous whole blood lead** is the test. Erythrocyte (zinc) protoporphyrin rises and was the traditional screening test, but it is insensitive at lower levels and blood lead has replaced it; metaphyseal lead lines on long-bone films and radio-opaque gut flecks are supportive.
- **Treatment:** stop exposure first — chelation during continuing exposure can increase absorption. Chelate symptomatic adults above about **70 µg/dL**, and children with encephalopathy or levels above about **45 µg/dL**. For encephalopathy or symptomatic poisoning: **dimercaprol (BAL) first, with the first EDTA dose at least 4 hours later**, because calcium disodium EDTA given alone can redistribute lead into the brain. Oral **succimer (DMSA)** is first choice for asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic elevations, including in children. BAL is given in peanut oil and causes haemolysis in G6PD deficiency; EDTA is nephrotoxic and needs good urine flow.

options.A: Red blood cells carry nearly all circulating lead, but with a half-life of 30–40 days they are a transport pool, not a reservoir.
options.B: Soft tissue (kidney, brain, liver) is where toxicity happens, with a half-life around 40 days — too fast to store a burden.
options.C: Correct. More than 90% of adult body lead, half-life 20–30 years, slowly exchangeable with blood.
options.D: Renal filtrate is an excretory route — about 75% of daily loss — not a storage site.

92.picks_note: You and HT both picked A. It is a defensible reflex: lead is measured in whole blood precisely because erythrocytes hold it, so "red cells" is where lead visibly lives. The stem defeats it with the word "continues to increase" — a compartment that clears in a month cannot accumulate while the blood level falls, and the only slow compartment offered is bone.

93.why: Lead blocks haem synthesis at two points. δ-Aminolevulinic acid dehydratase (ALA dehydrase, also called porphobilinogen synthase) converts ALA to porphobilinogen; inhibiting it dams ALA upstream, so serum and urine ALA rise. Ferrochelatase catalyses the last step, insertion of ferrous iron into protoporphyrin IX; inhibiting it leaves protoporphyrin unused, so erythrocyte protoporphyrin rises. The stem gives you both raised ALA and raised protoporphyrin — a block at the second step of the pathway and a block at the last one.
93.watch: D is the designed trap. ALA synthase (ALA synthetase) is the rate-limiting, haem-regulated first enzyme, and it is the enzyme most often named in haem-pathway questions — but lead does not inhibit it; if anything it is induced when haem falls. The enzyme lead hits is the next one down, the dehydratase. Keep the two names apart: **synthase makes ALA, dehydratase consumes it**, and only the second is a lead target.
93.hook: Lead squeezes haem synthesis at both ends — ALA dehydratase near the start, ferrochelatase at the finish — and both metabolites pile up where the squeeze is.
93.explain:
## Why the anaemia looks the way it does

Haem is built in eight steps that shuttle between mitochondrion and cytosol. Lead is a thiol-group poison, so it preferentially inactivates the zinc- and sulfhydryl-dependent enzymes of this pathway. Two matter clinically:

- **ALA dehydratase** blocked → ALA accumulates. ALA is structurally similar to GABA and is thought to contribute to the neurological features, which is why lead poisoning can mimic an acute porphyric attack (abdominal pain, neuropathy, psychiatric change) with a crucial difference: in lead, ALA is high but **porphobilinogen is not**, because the block is immediately before it.
- **Ferrochelatase** blocked → iron cannot be inserted into protoporphyrin IX, so zinc occupies the ring instead. The resulting rise in **erythrocyte (zinc) protoporphyrin** is the basis of the older screening test for chronic exposure — insensitive at low levels, so blood lead is now the test — and it also explains the ring (sideroblastic) pattern in marrow iron stains.

Iron delivery is impaired for a second reason as well: lead interferes with mobilisation of iron from stores, so the marrow is functionally iron-restricted while body iron is adequate or high. The anaemia is usually mild, microcytic or normocytic, and hypoproliferative in part — but the stem's reticulocytosis points to the other half of the mechanism: lead shortens red cell survival and increases mechanical fragility, so there is a haemolytic component.

## Neighbouring facts worth holding

- **Pyrimidine-5′-nucleotidase** is also inhibited. Undegraded RNA aggregates give the classic **basophilic stippling** on the film — a lead finding, but a red-cell one, not a haem-synthesis one.
- Distinguishing lead anaemia from iron deficiency: both can raise protoporphyrin, but lead leaves **ferritin and transferrin saturation normal or high**, and iron deficiency does not cause stippling.
- Sideroblastic anaemia has a small differential worth reciting — lead, isoniazid and other pyridoxine antagonists, chloramphenicol, alcohol, copper deficiency, zinc excess, and the hereditary ALAS2 defect.

options.A: Correct. The two lead-sensitive steps: ALA → porphobilinogen, and iron insertion into protoporphyrin IX.
options.B: Ferrochelatase is right, catalase is not a haem-pathway enzyme and is not the relevant target.
options.C: Pyrimidine-5′-nucleotidase is genuinely inhibited by lead, but it explains basophilic stippling, not the accumulation of ALA and protoporphyrin; catalase again does not belong.
options.D: The classic near-miss: ferrochelatase is correct but ALA synthetase is the wrong enzyme — lead blocks ALA dehydratase, one step later.

93.picks_note: Your pick, D, is the single most seductive option here, because ALA synthase is the enzyme everyone memorises from the porphyria pathway as the rate-limiting step; getting ferrochelatase right in the same option makes it feel confirmed. The stem's clue is the raised **ALA** itself: if the first enzyme were blocked, ALA could not accumulate. HT left it blank.

94.why: Carbon tetrachloride is not intrinsically hepatotoxic; it has to be activated. Hepatic cytochrome P450 (chiefly CYP2E1) reductively dechlorinates it to the trichloromethyl radical and then the trichloromethyl peroxy radical. These covalently bind cellular proteins and strip hydrogen from membrane lipids, propagating lipid peroxidation until membranes, including mitochondrial and endoplasmic reticulum membranes, fail. The injury is therefore metabolite-mediated, which is also why it is concentrated where P450 activity is highest.
94.watch: A sounds mechanistically respectable because mitochondrial dysfunction does occur — but it is downstream of radical-mediated membrane damage, not the initiating event. The test of a "mechanism" option is whether it explains the organ and the zone: only bioactivation by hepatic P450 explains why injury is hepatic and centrilobular.
94.hook: Carbon tetrachloride poisons the liver only after the liver has activated it — the toxin is the metabolite.
94.explain:
## Exposure to lesion

Absorption is through lungs, skin and gut, and the solvent concentrates in adipose tissue. About half the absorbed dose is exhaled unchanged; most of the rest is metabolised in the liver. Two organ patterns follow.

- **Liver:** fatty (steatotic) degeneration at lower exposures, **centrilobular (zone 3) necrosis** at higher ones. Zone 3 is hit because CYP2E1 is densest there and oxygen tension lowest — exactly the explanation for paracetamol and halothane injury too. Transaminases peak over 2–4 days; jaundice, coagulopathy and acute liver failure can follow.
- **Kidney:** acute tubular necrosis affecting proximal tubule and loop of Henle, which can dominate the later course and sometimes appears with only modest hepatic injury.
- **Heart and CNS:** immediate deaths are not hepatic. Like other halogenated hydrocarbons, carbon tetrachloride **sensitises the myocardium to circulating catecholamines**, causing ventricular dysrhythmias, and acutely it is a CNS depressant with narcosis and headache.

## What modifies the injury

Anything that induces CYP2E1 multiplies toxicity — **ethanol** is the classic, also isoniazid and fasting — because more substrate is converted to radical. Management is supportive: remove from exposure, decontaminate skin, avoid catecholamines where possible given myocardial sensitisation, and watch liver and renal function for several days. **N-acetylcysteine** is used on the rationale of restoring glutathione and scavenging radicals; evidence is limited but the risk is low. Hyperbaric oxygen has been tried and is not established.

## File it with its relatives

The radical-generating, zone-3 pattern links carbon tetrachloride, chloroform, halothane and paracetamol. Among toxic causes of acute liver failure, keep it alongside *Amanita phalloides* and yellow phosphorus, which Indian examiners favour.

options.A: Mitochondrial injury happens, but as a consequence of radical-mediated lipid peroxidation rather than as the primary mechanism.
options.B: Correct. P450-generated trichloromethyl radicals bind proteins and drive lipid peroxidation, producing centrilobular necrosis.
options.C: Renal tubular accumulation describes the kidney lesion, which does not account for hepatic injury.
options.D: Catecholamine sensitisation explains early arrhythmic deaths, not hepatocellular damage.

95.why: A serum iron at or above 500 µg/dL is itself an indication for chelation, independent of how well the patient looks. Above roughly that level, binding capacity is exceeded and free iron circulates to uncouple oxidative phosphorylation and catalyse free-radical injury in liver, heart and vessels. At 560 µg/dL this patient has crossed the biochemical threshold, and the absence of shock, acidosis or coma is not reassurance — it is compatible with the deceptive latent phase that precedes stage III.
95.watch: Observation (B) is the trap built into the stem, because the patient is described as asymptomatic and most iron ingestions genuinely are benign. The point of the stage structure is that the quiet interval between 6 and 24 hours is when an untreated serious poisoning looks best. Severe clinical features are an indication for deferoxamine regardless of the level; a high level is an indication regardless of the features. Either route suffices.
95.hook: In iron poisoning, a patient who looks well with an iron of 560 is not reassuring — they are in the latent phase, and they are chelated on the number.
95.explain:
## Why iron kills in stages

Iron is directly corrosive to gut mucosa, and once absorbed in excess it saturates transferrin; free ferric iron then enters mitochondria, uncouples oxidative phosphorylation, and generates radicals that peroxidate membranes. Hepatocytes and the vasculature take the brunt, and the lactic acidosis comes from both the mitochondrial block and shock.

- **Stage I (0–6 h):** vomiting, diarrhoea, haematemesis, abdominal pain — corrosive. Absence of GI symptoms in the first 6 hours effectively excludes a serious ingestion.
- **Stage II (6–24 h):** apparent recovery. The dangerous window for false reassurance.
- **Stage III:** shock, high anion gap metabolic acidosis, hepatic necrosis, coagulopathy, coma.
- **Stage IV (2–3 days):** fulminant hepatic failure.
- **Stage V (2–6 weeks):** gastric outlet or small bowel stricture from the healing corrosive injury.

## The numbers and the practicalities

- Toxicity relates to **elemental** iron: under 20 mg/kg is usually benign, 20–60 mg/kg gives gastrointestinal symptoms, above 60 mg/kg risks systemic toxicity, and above about 120 mg/kg is potentially lethal.
- Serum iron is taken at **4–6 hours**, when it peaks (later with sustained-release preparations). Below 300 µg/dL is generally mild; 500 µg/dL and above indicates systemic toxicity. Total iron-binding capacity adds nothing in acute poisoning and should not be used to guide treatment.
- **Activated charcoal does not bind iron.** Whole bowel irrigation with polyethylene glycol is the decontamination option for large ingestions or a radiographically visible tablet mass; gastrotomy is occasionally needed for an adherent bezoar.
- **Deferoxamine** 15 mg/kg/h by infusion, chelating free iron to ferrioxamine, which is renally excreted and turns the urine the classic "vin rosé" shade. Watch for **hypotension** if infused too fast, and for **ARDS** with infusions beyond about 24 hours; *Yersinia* sepsis is the other reported complication. Stop when acidosis has resolved, the patient is clinically well, and urine colour has normalised.
- Haemodialysis does not remove iron, but it does remove the ferrioxamine complex and so has a role only in renal failure.

options.A: Correct. Serum iron ≥500 µg/dL is a stated indication for chelation even in an asymptomatic patient.
options.B: Wrong because of the number, and because stage II looks exactly like this. Observation alone is for low levels with no significant GI phase.
options.C: Charcoal does not adsorb iron; repeat dosing achieves nothing.
options.D: Dialysis does not clear iron itself and is reserved for removing the deferoxamine–iron complex in renal failure.

95.picks_note: HT picked B. It is the intuitive reading of a stem that lists everything the patient does not have — no shock, no acidosis, no altered consciousness — which sounds like permission to watch. The single number 560 µg/dL overrides all of it, and the stem's "otherwise asymptomatic" is the exact phrase the threshold was written for.

key.note: Standard texts give both routes to chelation: severe clinical toxicity at any level, or serum iron ≥500 µg/dL when asymptomatic. Modern practice weights the clinical picture first, but the 500 threshold is still the quoted cut-off.

96.why: Pyridoxine is dosed gram-for-gram with the isoniazid ingested when the amount is known, so 6 g of isoniazid means 6 g of intravenous pyridoxine. The specified rate is about 1 g per minute, which puts the infusion at roughly 6 minutes. Speed is part of the prescription: these seizures do not stop until the pyridoxine arrives, and the published experience of rapid gram-for-gram dosing is termination of seizures, shortened coma and faster resolution of the acidosis.
96.watch: D has the right dose and the wrong tempo, and in status epilepticus the tempo is the treatment — an hour-long infusion leaves the patient seizing for an hour. B (5 g) is the dose for an **unknown** ingestion; here the quantity is given, so the gram-for-gram rule applies. A applies a paediatric 70 mg/kg cap to an adult stem.
96.hook: Grams of isoniazid in, grams of pyridoxine back, at a gram a minute — and a correct dose given too slowly is still a wrong answer.
96.explain:
## Why benzodiazepines alone fail

Isoniazid and its hydrazine metabolites bind pyridoxal-5′-phosphate and inhibit pyridoxine kinase. Pyridoxal phosphate is the cofactor for glutamic acid decarboxylase, the enzyme that makes GABA from glutamate. So the brain stops synthesising its principal inhibitory transmitter. Benzodiazepines work by potentiating GABA at its receptor — if there is no GABA to potentiate, they have little to act on, which is exactly why isoniazid seizures are described as refractory and why the preferred regimen is **pyridoxine plus a benzodiazepine** rather than either alone: replacing the cofactor restores the transmitter, and the benzodiazepine then works.

The second limb of toxicity is metabolic. Hydrazines also block lactate conversion and NADH-dependent steps, so the classic acute overdose triad is **refractory seizures, a high anion gap (lactic) metabolic acidosis, and coma**. The acidosis is largely seizure-driven and resolves once the convulsions stop; chasing it with bicarbonate instead of pyridoxine is a standard error.

## The numbers to hold

- **Known ingestion:** pyridoxine 1 g IV per gram of isoniazid. Rate: this item's source says about **1 g/min**; other toxicology sources say 0.5–1 g/min and cap the total at 5 g, giving any remainder over the next few hours. Either way the first grams go in over minutes, not an hour.
- **Unknown ingestion:** at least **5 g** IV in adults (70 mg/kg in children, commonly capped at 5 g). Give it empirically in any seizing patient on antituberculous treatment — India's prescribing patterns make this a realistic bedside call.
- If intravenous pyridoxine is not stocked, crushed oral tablets by nasogastric tube are the fallback; pharmacy stock is the real-world rate-limiting step.
- **Avoid phenytoin** — ineffective in toxic seizures and its metabolism is inhibited by isoniazid. Escalate instead to barbiturates or propofol, with intubation and neuromuscular blockade for refractory status, remembering that paralysis hides seizures and needs EEG.
- Isoniazid has a small volume of distribution (~0.6 L/kg) and low protein binding, so it is dialysable — but dialysis is reserved for refractory cases or renal failure, because pyridoxine works faster.
- Chronic toxicity is a different exam: dose-dependent hepatitis, and peripheral neuropathy prevented by 10–25 mg/day of prophylactic pyridoxine.

options.A: 420 mg is 70 mg/kg for a 6 kg child — a paediatric cap misapplied, and far below the needed dose here.
options.B: 5 g is the empirical dose when the ingested amount is unknown; here it is known, and 30 minutes is too slow for status.
options.C: Correct. Gram-for-gram with 6 g ingested, infused at about 1 g/min.
options.D: Right dose, wrong rate — 60 minutes abandons the patient in status epilepticus.

96.picks_note: Your pick, B, is the dose you would reach for in the far commoner real scenario of an unknown quantity, and 30 minutes feels like safe practice; the stem deliberately tells you the exact 6 g so that the gram-for-gram rule is the one being tested. HT picked A, the paediatric 70 mg/kg ceiling applied to an adult — a number worth keeping, but attached to the wrong patient.

key.note: Key is right among these options. Note one honest variation: several toxicology sources cap total pyridoxine at 5 g and infuse at 0.5 g/min, which would make 5 g defensible as a dose — but not over 30 minutes in status epilepticus, so C remains the answer.

98.answer: B. Amiodarone (this bank and Irwin & Rippe). Current toxicology practice favours a titrated short-acting beta-blocker such as esmolol.
98.why: Of the four options, only two are antiarrhythmics at all, and only amiodarone is an answer the bank will accept: the source text recommends amiodarone or lidocaine when theophylline toxicity produces ventricular irritability with haemodynamic compromise. Adenosine acts at the AV node and treats supraventricular tachycardia; cimetidine is not an antiarrhythmic and is relatively contraindicated because it inhibits theophylline metabolism and deepens the toxicity. So B is the defensible pick under exam conditions.
98.watch: Esmolol is the option to think hardest about, because by mechanism it is arguably the better drug — theophylline dysrhythmias are catecholamine-driven, and beta-blockade treats the cause rather than the rhythm. The exam's logic is narrower: it treats esmolol as the answer for selected tachydysrhythmias and amiodarone or lidocaine as the answer for ventricular irritability with compromise. Recognise the key, and know why the toxicology literature disagrees.
98.hook: Theophylline arrhythmias are a catecholamine storm, so the mechanism-matched drug is a titratable beta-blocker — but this bank keys amiodarone.
98.explain:
## Where the toxicity comes from

Theophylline does two things at once: it antagonises adenosine receptors and it inhibits phosphodiesterase, raising cyclic AMP. The result is a massive endogenous catecholamine surge with beta-receptor stimulation, which explains nearly every feature — sinus and supraventricular tachycardia then ventricular ectopy, vasodilatation with a wide pulse pressure and hypotension, tremor and agitation, vomiting, and the metabolic signature of **hypokalaemia, hypophosphataemia, hypomagnesaemia, hyperglycaemia and lactic acidosis**. The hypokalaemia is intracellular shift, not deficit, so it corrects as toxicity resolves; aggressive replacement risks rebound hyperkalaemia. Seizures are the feared neurological complication, carry high mortality, and are treated with benzodiazepines then barbiturates — phenytoin is ineffective.

## Acute versus chronic matters

Acute overdose produces the highest levels and the most vomiting and metabolic derangement, but seizures and arrhythmias correlate poorly with the level. **Chronic** toxicity — the elderly patient whose clearance has fallen because of heart failure, liver disease, or an interacting drug such as cimetidine, erythromycin, ciprofloxacin or a fluvoxamine — causes seizures and arrhythmias at much lower levels, sometimes from 40–60 mg/L. Know the interaction list; it is the commonest real-world mechanism.

## Treatment, with the disagreement stated plainly

- **Decontamination:** activated charcoal, and theophylline is a prime indication for **multi-dose** charcoal because of enterohepatic and enterocapillary recirculation.
- **Rhythm and pressure:** fluids first for hypotension, then a vasoconstrictor such as phenylephrine or noradrenaline. For tachydysrhythmias, modern toxicology texts recommend a **short-acting beta-blocker (esmolol 0.05 mg/kg/min, titrated)** for both supraventricular and ventricular rhythms, because the hypotension is itself beta-2-mediated vasodilatation, so removing beta stimulation raises the pressure and corrects the potassium shift as well; it is used cautiously in patients with asthma or COPD, who are, inconveniently, the people on theophylline. Irwin & Rippe, and therefore this bank, recommend **amiodarone or lidocaine** for ventricular irritability with compromise and reserve esmolol for selected tachydysrhythmias. **Current: titrated esmolol is mechanistically preferred. Older keys and this bank: amiodarone or lidocaine.**
- **Extracorporeal removal:** theophylline is an ideal candidate — small molecule, low protein binding, small volume of distribution. Indications are level above about **100 mg/L** in acute overdose or **60 mg/L** in chronic toxicity (**50 mg/L** if over 60 years or under 6 months), or severe toxicity at any level — seizures, life-threatening dysrhythmia, or shock. Intermittent haemodialysis is now preferred over charcoal haemoperfusion, which is the alternative only when dialysis is unavailable.
- **Avoid** cimetidine and any other clearance inhibitor.

options.A: Adenosine works at the AV node and is for supraventricular tachycardia, not ventricular irritability with compromise.
options.B: The keyed answer: amiodarone (or lidocaine) for theophylline-induced ventricular irritability with haemodynamic compromise.
options.C: Esmolol is the mechanism-matched drug in current toxicology practice, and the strongest challenge to the key; the bank treats it as reserved for selected tachydysrhythmias and cautions about bronchospasm.
options.D: Cimetidine is not an antiarrhythmic and inhibits theophylline metabolism — relatively contraindicated.

key.note: Current toxicology sources (Goldfrank's and standard critical care toxicology practice) recommend a titrated short-acting beta-blocker, usually esmolol, for theophylline-induced supraventricular and ventricular tachydysrhythmias, since they are catecholamine-mediated. Irwin & Rippe, the source of this item, keys amiodarone or lidocaine. Answer B in the exam; know the esmolol argument.

99.answer: B. Oral Gastrografin (1 mL/kg) — the protocol this item is drawn from.
99.why: The question asks for the first step of the quoted protocol in a patient who is stable with no sign of rupture, and that protocol is deliberately non-invasive: a water-soluble oral contrast agent at 1 mL/kg, followed by abdominal imaging to locate the packets and then serial imaging to confirm they are passing. Everything surgical or endoscopic in the options belongs to the patient who has become symptomatic, which this one has not.
99.watch: Immediate laparotomy is the answer to a different stem — the body packer who develops sudden sympathomimetic toxicity, because a ruptured cocaine packet has no antidote and surgery is the only way to stop the delivery. Here the stem spends a whole sentence telling you the patient is stable with no evidence of rupture, which is the examiner removing that option by hand.
99.hook: Asymptomatic packer: image and let the packets pass. Symptomatic packer: that is when the knife comes out.
99.explain:
## Packer against stuffer

A **body packer** swallows professionally wrapped packets for transport — many of them, well sealed, large doses, usually cocaine or heroin. A **body stuffer** hurriedly swallows poorly wrapped drug to escape arrest — fewer packets, smaller doses, far likelier to leak early. The packer's danger is therefore delayed and catastrophic; the stuffer's is early and usually survivable.

## The asymptomatic patient

- **Confirm and count.** **Unenhanced abdominal CT**, usually at a reduced dose, is the most reliable test; plain radiographs have a reported sensitivity anywhere from about 75% to 100% and a negative film cannot be used to declare a patient clear. Note the honest discrepancy with this item: the protocol it quotes starts with oral water-soluble contrast, whereas radiology reviews find that oral or intravenous contrast of density similar to the packets can markedly **hamper** their detection. Answer the question as asked; image with unenhanced CT.
- **Promote passage.** Whole bowel irrigation with polyethylene glycol until the effluent is clear and imaging shows no retained packets. Oil-based laxatives and enemas are avoided: they can dissolve the packet casing.
- **Observe where the drug can be treated.** Continuous monitoring, intravenous access, and naloxone ready for an opioid leak.
- **Do not endoscope** packets that have left the stomach; endoscopic retrieval risks rupturing them and is considered only for packets still gastric.

## When to operate

Any new symptom in a body packer is treated as rupture until proved otherwise. **Cocaine rupture** is a surgical emergency — agitation, hypertension, hyperthermia, seizures, wide-complex tachycardia and arrest, with no antidote and a dose that keeps absorbing; laparotomy removes the source. **Heroin rupture** is pharmacologically treatable: a naloxone infusion buys time and surgery is usually avoidable. Mechanical indications — obstruction, perforation, packets that will not move — also take the patient to theatre.

## Cocaine-specific points that pair with this

Avoid pure beta-blockade (unopposed alpha stimulation); use benzodiazepines generously, nitrates or phentolamine for hypertension and chest pain, sodium bicarbonate for a wide QRS, and active cooling for hyperthermia.

options.A: Immediate laparotomy is for suspected rupture, obstruction or perforation — none of which this stem offers.
options.B: Correct for the protocol asked about: oral water-soluble contrast 1 mL/kg before imaging, with serial follow-up.
options.C: Enemas are not part of any protocol and oil-based preparations risk dissolving packet casings.
options.D: Endoscopic retrieval is reserved for packets still in the stomach and risks rupturing them; it is not the opening step.

99.picks_note: Your pick, A, is the right answer attached to the wrong patient — laparotomy is exactly what a cocaine packer with sudden collapse needs, and that version of the stem is GT 7 Q101. HT picked C: serial enemas feel like they belong to a "help the packets along" strategy, but the agent that does that job is polyethylene glycol from above, and oil-based enemas are specifically contraindicated.

key.note: Protocol-bound item: the key follows the Irwin & Rippe management algorithm. Current radiology and toxicology practice starts with low-dose non-contrast abdominal CT, and advises against oral contrast because it can reduce sensitivity for cocaine packets.

100.why: Every complication listed in the stem is manufactured by the contractions themselves. Sustained maximal muscle activity consumes oxygen, generates lactate, produces heat faster than it can be lost, and breaks down myocytes, so hyperthermia, acidosis and a rising creatine kinase are downstream of one event. Benzodiazepines interrupt that event: they potentiate GABA-mediated inhibition in the spinal cord, restoring the inhibitory brake that strychnine has removed, and in high doses may also displace strychnine from glycine receptors. Stop the spasms and the cascade stops with them.
100.watch: The three rival options are all elimination strategies, and all are defeated by the same number: strychnine has a large volume of distribution, so there is very little of it in the blood to remove. Haemodialysis and charcoal haemoperfusion cannot clear a drug that sits in tissue, and urinary alkalinisation does nothing because renal elimination of strychnine is minimal — it is metabolised hepatically. Alkalinisation has a role in this patient only for the myoglobin, and that is treating the consequence rather than the cause.
100.hook: In strychnine poisoning the spasm is the disease — sedate it and the acidosis, the fever and the rhabdomyolysis are all being treated at once.
100.explain:
## The lesion

Strychnine is a competitive antagonist at the **glycine receptor** on postsynaptic motor neurons in the spinal cord and brainstem. Glycine is the main inhibitory transmitter at that level, so blocking it leaves the final common pathway permanently disinhibited: any stimulus — noise, touch, light — recruits every muscle group at once, agonist and antagonist together. Onset is within 15–30 minutes of ingestion.

The resulting picture is distinctive: generalised extensor spasms, opisthotonus, **risus sardonicus**, neck and jaw rigidity during the spasm, exquisite hyperacusis and hyperreflexia — and, because the lesion is below the cortex, **the patient is fully conscious and in pain throughout**.

## Separating it from tetanus

They look nearly identical during a spasm. The difference is between spasms: in strychnine poisoning the muscles **relax completely** in the intervals and trismus is not persistent, whereas tetanus maintains tonic rigidity and continuous trismus between paroxysms. Tetanus also has a days-long incubation with autonomic instability, against strychnine's onset in minutes. That distinction was GT 7 Q29.

## Management

- **Minimise stimulation**: a dark, quiet room; handle the patient as little as possible.
- **Benzodiazepines first**, in generous doses, titrated to abolition of spasm. Escalate to propofol or a barbiturate.
- If spasms continue, **intubate, paralyse with a non-depolarising blocker and ventilate**. This is both airway control — sustained chest wall and diaphragmatic contraction causes hypoventilation and hypoxia, and respiratory failure is the usual mode of death — and definitive spasm control. Remember that paralysis abolishes the visible sign while leaving the patient awake: sedate adequately.
- **Active cooling** for hyperthermia; fluids, with urinary alkalinisation as an adjunct, for rhabdomyolysis; monitor potassium and renal function.
- **Activated charcoal** early if the airway is secure. Elimination enhancement has no role.

## One line of context

Strychnine is a rodenticide alkaloid from *Strychnos nux-vomica*, and in Indian practice it also turns up as an adulterant. In rodenticide classifications it sits in the highly toxic group with arsenic, yellow phosphorus and metal phosphides.

options.A: Haemodialysis is futile: a large volume of distribution keeps the drug out of the blood compartment.
options.B: Urinary alkalinisation does not enhance elimination, since renal clearance of strychnine is minimal; it is useful here only against myoglobinuria.
options.C: Correct. Terminating the spasms removes the cause of the acidosis, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis and respiratory compromise.
options.D: Charcoal haemoperfusion fails for the same pharmacokinetic reason as dialysis.

100.picks_note: Your pick, B, treats the complication that is most visible in the stem — the rising creatine kinase — and alkalinisation is the correct reflex for myoglobinuria; the stem asks which intervention interrupts the **cascade**, and the cascade begins at the muscle contraction, not the kidney. HT guessed D, which fails on volume of distribution — the same argument GT 7 Q97 used to rule out dialysis in amlodipine poisoning.

101.why: Phencyclidine makes muscle work hard for hours: generalised rigidity, twitching, grimacing and slow writhing (athetoid) movements that can continue for more than ten hours. Sustained contraction uses up muscle ATP, the cell membrane fails and the cell contents (creatine kinase, myoglobin, potassium) leak into the blood. The stem has already told you the creatine kinase is markedly raised, so the complication to anticipate is rhabdomyolysis and the kidney injury that follows it.
101.watch: The phrase 'appears relatively calm' is the trap. In phencyclidine poisoning muscle injury tracks the rigidity and abnormal movements, not how agitated the patient looks, so a quiet patient can still be breaking down muscle. Status epilepticus sounds like a natural next step but generalised seizures are uncommon with this drug.
101.hook: Phencyclidine: judge muscle injury by the creatine kinase, not by how calm the patient looks.
101.explain:
## What the drug does
Phencyclidine (PCP, "angel dust") is a dissociative anaesthetic, the parent compound of ketamine. Its main action is to block the NMDA glutamate receptor channel, which disconnects the cortex from incoming sensation: the patient is awake, eyes open, but detached and insensitive to pain. It also blocks reuptake of dopamine and noradrenaline, which adds a sympathomimetic layer (hypertension, tachycardia, hyperthermia) and psychosis. Behaviour swings unpredictably between blank calm and sudden violence, and because the patient feels no pain, injuries are common.

## Why the muscle breaks down
The motor picture is one of overactivity: rigidity, tremor, facial grimacing, twitching around the mouth, jerky or athetoid movements, sometimes dystonic posturing. This muscle work continues even when behaviour has settled. Add hyperthermia, physical restraint and trauma, and rhabdomyolysis follows. Myoglobin then injures the kidney, so the dangerous sequence is rigidity, raised creatine kinase, myoglobinuria, acute kidney injury and hyperkalaemia.

## What else an examiner could pick
- **Eyes:** nystagmus (horizontal, vertical or rotatory) is the most useful sign. Pupils are usually normal in size and reactive; they may be small or large, but are not characteristically fixed.
- **Classic combination:** hypertension, nystagmus and bizarre or violent behaviour in a patient with a blank stare.
- **Seizures:** generalised seizures and status epilepticus occur but are uncommon.
- **Treatment:** there is no antidote. A quiet room and benzodiazepines control agitation and muscle activity; cool actively; give generous isotonic fluid for the rhabdomyolysis. Avoid physical restraint where possible because struggling worsens muscle injury and temperature.
- **Old trap:** acidifying the urine does increase PCP excretion (it is a weak base) but is not done, because acid urine promotes myoglobin precipitation in the tubules.

options.A: Correct. Hours of rigidity and involuntary movement injure muscle regardless of behaviour; the raised creatine kinase in the stem is the early signal.
options.B: Seizures can occur with phencyclidine, but generalised seizures and status epilepticus are uncommon, and nothing in the stem points to them.
options.C: Pupils are usually normal and reactive; they may be small or large. Nystagmus, not fixed miosis, is the characteristic eye sign.
options.D: The neuromuscular picture is overactivity: rigidity, twitching and athetosis. Flaccid paralysis is the opposite.

104.why: GFAP is a structural filament protein found almost only in astrocytes, so a rise in blood is specific to brain injury. It is released quickly when astrocytes are disrupted, which makes it useful both after head trauma and in stroke, where it rises early in intracerebral haemorrhage and later, more slowly, in ischaemic infarction. Oh's singles it out as the most promising marker across traumatic brain injury and both stroke types.
104.watch: All four options are real brain-injury markers, so the question is decided by which one the text highlights, not by any being 'wrong'. HT's pick, CK-BB, is the oldest and least specific of the four.
104.hook: GFAP comes only from astrocytes, which is why it is the marker pushed for TBI and for telling haemorrhage from infarct.
104.explain:
## Why a blood marker of brain injury is hard to find
A useful marker has to come from brain and nowhere else, cross into blood quickly, and scale with the amount of injury. Most candidates fail the first test. Your card PCA-47 already covers the two used after cardiac arrest: neuron-specific enolase (NSE) from neurons and S-100B from glia. This card adds the trauma and stroke markers.

## The markers and their weak points
- **NSE:** from neuronal cytoplasm, but also present in red cells and platelets, so a haemolysed sample gives a false high. Also raised in small-cell lung cancer and neuroendocrine tumours.
- **S-100B:** from astrocytes, but also from fat, cartilage and skin, so it rises with fractures and polytrauma without any brain injury. Its strength is a high negative predictive value: a low value within about 6 hours of a mild head injury is used in the Scandinavian guidelines to avoid a CT.
- **CK-BB:** the brain isoenzyme of creatine kinase; present in astrocytes but also in gut, bladder and prostate. Low specificity; largely of historical interest.
- **GFAP:** astrocyte cytoskeleton, essentially brain-specific. Rises within an hour of injury.
- **UCH-L1** (ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolase L1): a neuronal enzyme, usually paired with GFAP.

## What NEET could ask next
- The GFAP plus UCH-L1 blood test is the first FDA-cleared brain-injury assay: in adults with mild TBI (GCS 13 to 15) sampled within 12 hours, a negative result predicts a normal CT.
- Measured on the day of injury, GFAP and UCH-L1 also carry prognostic information in moderate to severe TBI.
- In acute stroke, an early high GFAP favours intracerebral haemorrhage over infarction, because haemorrhage destroys astrocytes at once while infarcted tissue releases GFAP over a day or two.
- After cardiac arrest the guideline marker is still NSE (above 60 µg/L at 48 or 72 hours), with neurofilament light chain the newer addition.
- No marker replaces examination and imaging.

options.A: A neuronal marker, best validated for prognosis after cardiac arrest. Falsely raised by haemolysis; not the one highlighted for trauma and stroke.
options.B: Glial, with good negative predictive value in mild head injury, but released from fat and bone as well, so it is not brain-specific.
options.C: The brain isoenzyme of creatine kinase. An old, non-specific marker also released from gut and bladder.
options.D: Correct. Astrocyte-specific, rises early, useful in TBI and in both ischaemic and haemorrhagic stroke.

104.picks_note: HT picked C, CK-BB. It is a genuine brain-derived enzyme and the 'BB' label makes it sound specific, but it is also found in gut, bladder and prostate and is not the marker any current text promotes.

key.note: Passage-based: the stem asks which marker is 'highlighted' in Oh's. GFAP is also the best answer on current evidence.

105.why: A structural lesion (bleed, infarct, tumour, abscess) damages one place, so it produces signs on one side or at one level: a hemiparesis, a unilateral extensor plantar, a blown pupil. A metabolic or toxic cause reaches every neuron through the blood, so its signs are symmetrical. The patient in the stem looks metabolic so far (reactive pupils, myoclonus, tremor); the finding that would overturn that impression is asymmetry.
105.watch: Asterixis feels like a 'hard' neurological sign, but it belongs to the metabolic list along with tremor and multifocal myoclonus. Fluctuating consciousness is also metabolic.
105.hook: Coma with reactive pupils and symmetrical signs is metabolic until proved otherwise; asymmetry means image the brain now.
105.explain:
## Why coma has only two anatomical explanations
Wakefulness needs the ascending reticular activating system in the upper brainstem and at least one working cerebral hemisphere. Coma therefore means either both hemispheres are failing together or the brainstem activating system is hit. A diffuse process (hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, uraemia, liver failure, sepsis, drugs) does the first. A structural lesion does the second, either directly in the brainstem or by a hemispheric mass pushing down on it.

## Sorting them at the bedside
- **Pupils:** the pupillary light pathway runs through the midbrain next to the activating system but is relatively resistant to metabolic insult. Reactive pupils in a deeply comatose patient point to a metabolic cause; a fixed or unequal pupil points to a structural one. Exceptions that fix or distort the pupils without a lesion: anticholinergics (large, fixed), opioids and organophosphates (pinpoint), severe hypoxia, hypothermia, barbiturate overdose.
- **Motor signs:** symmetrical in metabolic coma, asymmetrical in structural.
- **Involuntary movements:** tremor, asterixis (brief loss of postural tone, the flapping tremor) and multifocal myoclonus are metabolic.
- **Course:** metabolic encephalopathy waxes and wanes and is often preceded by confusion; structural coma progresses in an orderly head-to-tail sequence as herniation advances.
- **Breathing and eye movements:** conjugate roving eye movements and intact oculocephalic reflexes favour metabolic; a gaze palsy or dysconjugate eyes favour structural.

## The classic exceptions
Hypoglycaemia, hepatic encephalopathy and non-ketotic hyperglycaemia can produce focal signs, including hemiparesis, so glucose is checked in every coma. In the other direction, bilateral or multifocal structural disease (subarachnoid haemorrhage, bilateral subdurals, venous sinus thrombosis, meningitis) can look symmetrical.

options.A: Fluctuation is typical of metabolic encephalopathy; it does not point to a lesion.
options.B: Symmetry is what a diffuse metabolic process produces.
options.C: Asterixis is a metabolic sign (liver failure, uraemia, CO₂ retention, drugs).
options.D: Correct. A one-sided deficit means one part of the brain is damaged, which is structural disease.

105.picks_note: HT picked C. Asterixis is striking to see but it only reinforces the metabolic picture the stem has already drawn; the question asks for the finding that argues against it.

107.why: The dominant hemisphere is the one that holds language, which is the left in nearly all right-handed people and most left-handed people. Damage to its middle cerebral artery territory gives aphasia, and with it the related disorders of writing (dysgraphia) and calculation (dyscalculia). The other three options all describe neglect of the left side, which is the signature of a non-dominant (right) hemisphere lesion.
107.watch: The stem is internally awkward: left hemiplegia, left hemianopia and eyes turned to the right already place the lesion in the right hemisphere, where left-sided neglect is the expected companion. The question is not asking what this patient is likely to have; it asks which sign, if present, would mean the affected hemisphere is the language-dominant one. Only B is a language sign, and A, C and D are three wordings of the same thing.
107.hook: Language signs mean dominant hemisphere; neglect means non-dominant. Three options that say the same thing cannot be the answer.
107.explain:
## Why the middle cerebral artery gives this picture
The middle cerebral artery supplies the lateral surface of the hemisphere and, through its deep branches, the internal capsule. One occlusion therefore takes out several things at once, all on the side opposite the lesion:

- **Weakness and sensory loss** of the face and arm more than the leg, because the leg area lies on the medial surface in anterior cerebral artery territory. If the deep branches to the internal capsule are involved, face, arm and leg are equally dense.
- **Homonymous hemianopia**, from the optic radiation.
- **Gaze deviation towards the lesion.** Each frontal eye field drives the eyes to the opposite side; when one is destroyed the intact one wins, so the eyes look at the damaged hemisphere and away from the paralysed limbs. (A seizure focus or a pontine lesion does the reverse.)

## What the side adds
- **Dominant (usually left):** aphasia. A frontal (Broca's) lesion gives non-fluent speech with preserved understanding; a temporal (Wernicke's) lesion gives fluent, empty speech with poor understanding; a whole-territory infarct gives global aphasia. A lesion of the dominant angular gyrus gives Gerstmann syndrome: agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia and left-right confusion.
- **Non-dominant (usually right):** neglect of the left half of space and of the left side of the body, unawareness of the deficit (anosognosia), and difficulty with dressing and drawing.

## What follows in the ICU
A large middle cerebral artery infarct swells, with oedema peaking around days 2 to 5 ("malignant" infarction). Decompressive hemicraniectomy within 48 hours in patients up to 60 years reduces mortality substantially. A non-dominant infarct is not a reason to withhold it, and a dominant one is not a contraindication.

options.A: Neglect of the left side is what a right, non-dominant hemisphere lesion produces.
options.B: Correct. Aphasia and dysgraphia are language functions, which live in the dominant hemisphere.
options.C: Another description of left hemispatial neglect: non-dominant.
options.D: Again left-sided neglect: non-dominant.

107.picks_note: Your pick, A. Left neglect is exactly what fits the patient described (a right hemisphere stroke), which is why it felt right. But the question asked for the sign of a dominant lesion, and neglect is the non-dominant sign; A, C and D being the same finding was the clue.

key.note: The stem describes a right-hemisphere syndrome and then asks for a dominant-hemisphere sign, so it is poorly constructed, but B is the only language sign and the only possible answer.

108.why: After 48 hours of hyponatraemia the brain has adapted by shedding its organic osmolytes, so a fast rise in sodium shrinks the cells and risks osmotic demyelination. Oh's therefore limits correction of chronic hyponatraemia to 0.5 mmol/L per hour and 8 mmol/L in 24 hours, with sodium checked every 4 hours. Seventy-two hours makes this chronic, so the slow limit applies.
108.watch: Two numbers are set against each other. 1 mmol/L/hour belongs to the first few hours of treating severe symptoms (seizure, coma), not to chronic correction. 8 is the correct figure but for a day, not an hour.
108.hook: Chronic hyponatraemia: no more than 0.5 an hour and 8 a day, and the daily limit is the one that matters.
108.explain:
## Reading the two limits together
Your cards ABE-11 and NA-08 explain why the adapted brain is harmed by fast correction. What this question adds is an hourly figure. Notice that 0.5 mmol/L per hour sustained for a day would be 12 mmol/L, which breaks the daily limit of 8. The hourly figure is only a ceiling on speed at any moment; the 24-hour total is what protects the patient. Current guidance no longer quotes an hourly rate and sets daily limits only: the European guideline allows 10 in the first 24 hours and 8 per day after that; the US expert panel allows 10 to 12 in 24 hours for ordinary risk and 8 for patients at high risk of demyelination. If an exam offers 0.5 per hour for chronic hyponatraemia, take it; if it offers a daily figure, take 8.

## Why SAH is different in one respect
Hyponatraemia after subarachnoid haemorrhage is usually from natriuresis (cerebral salt wasting) or SIADH. Fluid restriction is avoided because hypovolaemia promotes delayed cerebral ischaemia, so sodium is raised with fluid that is more concentrated than the patient's serum (hypertonic saline) and with fludrocortisone, while respecting the same limits.

options.A: Too fast for chronic hyponatraemia. Rates of 1 to 2 mmol/L/hour belong only to the first hours of treating severe symptoms, and even then the day's total stays within the limit.
options.B: Correct. The stated maximum hourly rate for hyponatraemia of more than 48 hours.
options.C: Far too fast; this would reach the daily limit in four hours.
options.D: 8 mmol/L is the maximum rise in 24 hours, not in one hour.

108.picks_note: Your pick, A. 1 mmol/L/hour is the figure remembered from emergency correction of symptomatic hyponatraemia. The stem says chronic (72 hours) and describes routine 4-hourly monitoring with no seizure or coma, so the slower limit applies. HT left it blank.

key.note: Passage-based ('in the supplied guidance', Oh's). Current guidelines (European 2014, US expert panel 2013) give daily limits rather than an hourly rate; the 8 mmol/L per day limit is the clinically binding one.

109.why: Ceftriaxone covers pneumococcus, meningococcus and Haemophilus but has no activity against Listeria monocytogenes. Listeria becomes a realistic cause of meningitis after the age of 50 and in anyone with impaired cell-mediated immunity, so ampicillin (or amoxicillin) 2 g every 4 hours is added in those groups. At 67 with no other risk factor, age alone is the reason.
109.watch: Vancomycin is also added to ceftriaxone in many regimens, but its reason is penicillin- and cephalosporin-resistant pneumococcus, which depends on local resistance and not on age. The stem asks specifically about the age-related pathogen. Meropenem is tempting because it does cover Listeria, but it is kept for post-neurosurgical and shunt infections.
109.hook: Over 50 or immunosuppressed: cephalosporins miss Listeria, so add ampicillin.
109.explain:
## Why a cephalosporin fails here
Your cards CNS-10 and CNS-24 give the organisms by age and the drug for each. The step linking them: Listeria's penicillin-binding proteins have poor affinity for all cephalosporins, so the organism is intrinsically resistant however sensitive it looks elsewhere. It is an intracellular bacterium controlled by T cells, which is why it appears when cell-mediated immunity is weak: neonates, pregnancy, age over 50, alcoholism, diabetes, malignancy, steroids and transplant recipients.

## The empirical regimen as a set of add-ons
- Base: ceftriaxone or cefotaxime, with dexamethasone given before or with the first dose.
- Age over 50 or impaired cellular immunity: add ampicillin or amoxicillin.
- Risk of resistant pneumococcus: add vancomycin (rifampicin is the alternative).
- After neurosurgery, shunt or penetrating trauma: vancomycin plus meropenem (or ceftazidime or cefepime), for staphylococci and Pseudomonas.

If Listeria is confirmed, treatment is for at least 21 days, co-trimoxazole is the alternative in penicillin allergy, and dexamethasone is stopped.

options.A: Rifampicin is an alternative partner to ceftriaxone for resistant pneumococcus; it is not Listeria cover.
options.B: Correct. The only option that covers Listeria and the standard age-based addition.
options.C: Meropenem, with vancomycin, is the regimen for neurosurgical or shunt-related meningitis; the stem excludes that history.
options.D: Added for cephalosporin-resistant pneumococcus according to local resistance, not because of age.

109.picks_note: HT picked C. Meropenem is broad and does have Listeria activity, so it looks like a safe upgrade, but the stem states there is no neurosurgical history, which is the setting meropenem is reserved for, and the question asks what accompanies ceftriaxone.

key.note: IDSA would give vancomycin as well as ampicillin in this age group; the stem's 'age-related pathogen spectrum' makes ampicillin the intended and correct answer.

110.why: Brain tissue oxygen tension is the partial pressure of oxygen in the few cubic millimetres of white matter around the probe tip, the balance between oxygen delivered and oxygen consumed. Normal is about 23 to 35 mm Hg in most texts (Oh's rounds it to about 40). Values below about 10 to 15 mm Hg correspond to ischaemia, and below 5 mm Hg the tissue is no longer viable. A reading of 4 mm Hg therefore falls in the cell-death range.
110.watch: Option B names a real threshold, but the PET-derived ischaemic threshold is 10 to 15 mm Hg, well above 4. 'Adequate systemic oxygenation' in the stem is there to stop you blaming the lungs: a normal arterial saturation does not guarantee local delivery.
110.hook: PbtO₂: about 40 normal, treat below 20, ischaemia at 10 to 15, cell death below 5.
110.explain:
## The ladder of values
Your card PERF-17 has the electrode, the normal range and the under-5 figure. This question tests the steps in between, as Oh's gives them:

- About 40 mm Hg: normal (most texts quote 23 to 35).
- Below 20 mm Hg: the threshold at which treatment is started in practice and in the trials.
- 10 to 15 mm Hg: the ischaemic threshold, validated against PET.
- 8.5 mm Hg: roughly equivalent to a jugular venous saturation of 50%, the ischaemic threshold for that monitor.
- Below 5 mm Hg: cell death.

## What to do with a low reading
First check the probe (a brief rise in FiO₂ should raise the value if it is working, and readings in the first hour or two after insertion are unreliable). Then look for the cause on each side of the balance: delivery (low cerebral perfusion pressure, raised ICP, vasospasm, hypocapnia from over-ventilation, anaemia, hypoxaemia) and demand (fever, seizures, pain). The reading is regional, so its meaning depends on whether the tip sits in normal-looking or injured brain.

options.A: Normal is around 40 mm Hg; 4 is a tenth of that.
options.B: The PET-defined ischaemic threshold is 10 to 15 mm Hg. A value of 4 is beyond ischaemia.
options.C: Correct. Values under 5 mm Hg are associated with cell death.
options.D: A PbtO₂ of about 8.5 mm Hg matches a jugular saturation of 50%, which is itself the ischaemic threshold, not normal (55 to 75%).

111.why: Delayed cerebral ischaemia is, by definition, delayed: it appears from about day 3 after aneurysm rupture, peaks around days 7 to 10, and the risk has passed by about day 21. It affects roughly 30% of patients and, with the infarcts it causes, is the main determinant of poor outcome in those who survive the initial bleed. The 21-day window is why nimodipine is given for 21 days.
111.watch: 'Results only from vasospasm' is the option built to catch the older teaching. Narrowing of large arteries on angiography is seen in up to 70% of patients, but only about 30% develop ischaemia, and ischaemia can occur without visible spasm.
111.hook: DCI: days 3 to 21, about 30% of patients, and more than vasospasm.
111.explain:
## Where this sits beside your cards
NEURO-71 gives the clinical definition (new focal deficit or a fall of 2 or more GCS points for at least an hour, other causes excluded) and the usual window of days 4 to 14. That is the peak-risk period used by AHA/ASA; Oh's quotes the outer limits, day 3 to day 21. Both are describing the same curve, and an exam option with either range is acceptable when the alternatives are 'within hours' or similar.

## Why it is not just spasm
Blood breakdown products in the subarachnoid space act on vessels of every size. Besides large-artery narrowing, the mechanisms are constriction of the microcirculation, microthrombi, inflammation, breakdown of the blood-brain barrier, loss of autoregulation, and cortical spreading depolarisation (waves of neuronal depolarisation with paradoxical vasoconstriction). This explains two facts examiners like: nimodipine improves outcome without reducing angiographic spasm, and clazosentan reduces angiographic spasm without improving outcome.

## The early period, for contrast
The first 72 hours belong to early brain injury: the surge in intracranial pressure at rupture, transient global ischaemia, acute hydrocephalus and rebleeding.

options.A: The first hours are dominated by raised ICP, hydrocephalus and rebleeding. DCI does not begin before about day 3.
options.B: About 30% develop DCI, not 5%.
options.C: Correct. The risk window runs from about day 3 to day 21, with the peak at days 7 to 10.
options.D: Large-vessel spasm is one mechanism among several; microvascular constriction, microthrombi, inflammation and spreading depolarisation also contribute.

111.picks_note: HT picked B. Five per cent is far too low for a complication described in the stem as responsible for a substantial share of poor outcomes; the figure is about 30%.

key.note: Oh's window is days 3–21; AHA/ASA 2023 and your cards quote the peak period, days 4–14. Not a conflict.

112.why: Pre-eclampsia starts with poor placental implantation in the first half of pregnancy, and low-dose aspirin is the only drug shown to reduce it. It works only if started while the placental vessels are still being remodelled, so it is begun before 16 weeks (ideally from 11 to 14 weeks) and continued until 34 to 36 weeks. A woman at 12 weeks identified as high risk is exactly the patient for it.
112.watch: Antioxidant vitamins have a plausible rationale (oxidative stress in the placenta) and were tested for that reason, but the trials were negative. WHO, NICE and FIGO all advise against them, and one large trial suggested harm (more prelabour rupture of membranes).
112.hook: High risk for pre-eclampsia: aspirin 150 mg at night, started before 16 weeks; add calcium only if dietary intake is low.
112.explain:
## Why aspirin, and why early
In normal pregnancy the trophoblast invades the spiral arteries and converts them into wide, low-resistance channels; this is complete by about 16 to 20 weeks. In pre-eclampsia the invasion is shallow, the placenta is under-perfused, and it releases anti-angiogenic factors that injure the mother's endothelium (your card OBS-17). One consequence is an imbalance between thromboxane A₂ from platelets, which constricts vessels and aggregates platelets, and prostacyclin from endothelium, which does the opposite. Low-dose aspirin irreversibly blocks platelet cyclo-oxygenase and so suppresses thromboxane while largely sparing endothelial prostacyclin. Given during placentation it improves the process; given after 16 weeks the benefit is much smaller.

## The numbers an examiner could use
- **Dose:** 150 mg daily, taken at night (FIGO, the ASPRE trial, Oh's). NICE gives 75 to 150 mg; ACOG uses 81 mg.
- **Timing:** start before 16 weeks (FIGO 11 to 14 weeks; NICE from 12 weeks). FIGO stops at 36 weeks (Oh's: at least 34 weeks) to limit bleeding at delivery; NICE and ACOG continue until birth.
- **Effect:** in ASPRE, preterm pre-eclampsia (before 37 weeks) fell by about 60%; term disease was not reduced.
- **Who is high risk (NICE):** one high-risk factor (hypertensive disease in a previous pregnancy, chronic hypertension, chronic kidney disease, SLE or antiphospholipid syndrome, type 1 or type 2 diabetes), or two or more moderate ones (first pregnancy, age 40 or more, interval over 10 years, BMI 35 or more, family history, multiple pregnancy). ACOG counts multiple pregnancy as a high-risk factor.
- **Calcium:** 1.5 to 2 g daily (WHO, FIGO), only where dietary calcium is low.
- **Not effective:** vitamins C and E, omega-3 or fish oil, metformin, low-molecular-weight heparin as routine, salt restriction, bed rest.

options.A: Correct. The dose and the early start are both the recommended ones.
options.B: Vitamins C and E did not prevent pre-eclampsia in trials and are not recommended.
options.C: Metformin has been studied in obese women but is not an established preventive.
options.D: Omega-3 supplementation has not been shown to prevent pre-eclampsia.

key.note: 150 mg is the FIGO/ASPRE/Oh's dose; NICE 75–150 mg, ACOG 81 mg. No other option is defensible.

115.why: TTP is caused by severe deficiency of ADAMTS13, the enzyme that trims von Willebrand factor, usually because of an autoantibody. Plasma exchange treats both halves of the problem: it removes the antibody and the ultra-large von Willebrand multimers, and the donor plasma supplies working enzyme. Steroids suppress further antibody production. Pregnancy does not change this, and because the disease is not caused by the placenta, delivering the baby does not cure it.
115.watch: Thrombotic microangiopathy in pregnancy invites the HELLP reflex of 'deliver'. That is right for HELLP and pre-eclampsia, which are placental diseases, and wrong for TTP unless plasma exchange fails or there is a fetal or obstetric reason.
115.hook: HELLP is cured by delivery; TTP is cured by plasma exchange, pregnant or not.
115.explain:
## What pregnancy adds to the TTP you know
Your cards PLT-09 and HEO-05 cover the picture (microangiopathic haemolysis, low platelets, normal clotting times, ADAMTS13 under 10%) and the rule against platelets. Pregnancy matters for three reasons.

- **It is a trigger.** von Willebrand factor rises and ADAMTS13 falls through normal pregnancy, so a borderline deficiency is unmasked, typically in the second or third trimester or postpartum. Congenital TTP (Upshaw-Schulman syndrome, no antibody) often presents for the first time in pregnancy and is treated with regular plasma infusion rather than exchange.
- **It must be told apart from HELLP and acute fatty liver.** In TTP the transaminases are near normal, clotting is normal, hypertension and proteinuria are not required, and ADAMTS13 is under 10%. It can occur before 20 weeks, which pre-eclampsia cannot.
- **Drug choices narrow.** Start plasma exchange on suspicion without waiting for the ADAMTS13 result, with methylprednisolone or oral prednisolone. Caplacizumab and rituximab have limited pregnancy data and are kept for refractory disease after specialist discussion.

options.A: Correct. Exchange removes the antibody and replaces ADAMTS13; steroids reduce antibody production.
options.B: Platelets feed the microthrombi and can precipitate stroke or myocardial infarction; given only for life-threatening bleeding.
options.C: Delivery treats placental disease (HELLP, pre-eclampsia), not TTP. It is reserved for failure of plasma exchange or fetal or obstetric indications, which the stem excludes.
options.D: Steroids alone leave the antibody and the multimers in the circulation; untreated TTP has a mortality of about 90%.

115.picks_note: HT picked D. Steroids are part of the regimen and avoiding an extracorporeal procedure in pregnancy sounds cautious, but plasma exchange is the life-saving component and is safe in pregnancy.

116.why: Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome is a thrombotic storm in small vessels driven by antiphospholipid antibodies and, downstream of them, by complement. First-line treatment is the combination the patient has already had: anticoagulation, corticosteroids and plasma exchange (or immunoglobulin). When thrombosis continues despite that, the next step is a targeted agent: eculizumab, which blocks complement C5, or rituximab, which depletes the B cells making the antibody.
116.watch: Termination or delivery feels logical because pregnancy is a recognised trigger, but once the cascade is running the antibodies and complement activation continue without the placenta. Delivery is for obstetric indications; it is not the treatment of the syndrome.
116.hook: CAPS: heparin, steroids and plasma exchange or IVIG first; eculizumab or rituximab when that fails.
116.explain:
## What is happening
Antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-β2-glycoprotein I) bind to endothelium, platelets and monocytes and switch them to a clotting state. Ordinary antiphospholipid syndrome gives a single large-vessel clot or a pregnancy loss. In fewer than 1% of patients a second hit, most often infection, then surgery, stopping anticoagulation, or pregnancy and the puerperium, sets off widespread small-vessel thrombosis with a cytokine storm and complement activation. Clots generate more thrombin and more inflammation, so the process feeds itself.

## How it is defined
All four are needed for definite disease: involvement of three or more organs; onset within one week; small-vessel occlusion on biopsy of at least one organ; and antiphospholipid antibodies present. Kidney, lung (ARDS), brain, heart and skin are the usual organs. The blood film often shows thrombocytopenia and schistocytes, so it mimics TTP, HELLP, DIC and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. Mortality is about 30 to 40% even with treatment.

## Why each treatment is there
- **Heparin:** stops clot extension and also inhibits complement; unfractionated heparin is preferred in the ICU.
- **High-dose steroids:** suppress the cytokine storm.
- **Plasma exchange and/or IVIG:** remove or neutralise the antibody and cytokines. Anticoagulation plus steroids plus one of these is "triple therapy" and gives the best survival.
- **Treat the trigger:** antibiotics for infection, debride necrotic tissue.
- **Cyclophosphamide:** added when CAPS occurs with active lupus.
- **Refractory disease:** rituximab or eculizumab. Eculizumab has reassuring pregnancy data from other complement diseases; it requires meningococcal vaccination or antibiotic cover.

Direct oral anticoagulants are avoided in antiphospholipid syndrome, and warfarin is used long term after recovery (not during pregnancy).

options.A: Platelets add fuel to a thrombotic process; avoided unless there is life-threatening bleeding.
options.B: Aspirin has a role in prevention in obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome, but alone it is no treatment for fulminant multi-organ thrombosis.
options.C: Correct. Complement blockade is the recognised step for disease refractory to triple therapy, alongside rituximab.
options.D: Ending the pregnancy does not switch off the antibody and complement cascade; delivery is decided on obstetric grounds.

116.picks_note: You and HT both picked D. Pregnancy is a known precipitant, so removing it looks like source control, and it is the right instinct in HELLP. In CAPS the thrombosis is self-sustaining once started, and the stem's wording, 'refractory disease' after three named therapies, was asking for the next drug.

key.note: Rituximab is the equally accepted alternative for refractory CAPS; it is not among the options.

117.why: By the third trimester the uterus has pushed the diaphragm up by about 4 cm. A drain placed in the usual fifth intercostal space could pass through the diaphragm into the liver or spleen, or into the abdomen. The drain is therefore placed one or two spaces higher than usual, in the third or fourth space, still in the mid-axillary to anterior axillary line.
117.watch: The rule is 'one to two spaces higher than usual', and usual is the fifth space. The second space is too high and is a different site altogether: the mid-clavicular second space is the old landmark for needle decompression, not for a drain.
117.hook: Chest drain in late pregnancy: fifth space becomes third or fourth, because the diaphragm has risen 4 cm.
117.explain:
## The principle
Your card PLEU-12 gives the usual drain site, the safe triangle at the fifth intercostal space. Resuscitate the mother first; the fetus depends entirely on her circulation. What changes in pregnancy is anatomy and physiology, and each change has a practical consequence.

## Changes that alter trauma care
- **Diaphragm up about 4 cm:** chest drain in the third or fourth intercostal space. After blunt trauma also think of a ruptured diaphragm with abdominal contents in the chest; explore with a finger before inserting the tube.
- **Aortocaval compression:** after about 20 weeks the uterus compresses the vena cava and aorta when she lies flat, cutting cardiac output by up to 30%. Displace the uterus to the left by hand, or tilt the whole spinal board 15 to 30 degrees to the left.
- **Blood volume up 40 to 50%:** she can lose 1.2 to 1.5 litres before her pulse and pressure change. The uterine circulation constricts first, so fetal distress may be the earliest sign of maternal shock.
- **Baseline values shift:** resting heart rate is 10 to 15 higher, PaCO₂ about 30 mm Hg (a 'normal' 40 means she is failing), fibrinogen is high (a 'normal' level of 2 g/L is low for pregnancy).
- **Airway and breathing:** functional residual capacity down 20% and oxygen consumption up, so she desaturates fast; oedematous airway and delayed gastric emptying make intubation harder and aspiration likelier.
- **Access:** above the diaphragm.

## Pregnancy-specific injuries and steps
- Placental abruption is a leading cause of fetal loss when the mother survives; it can follow minor trauma and be concealed, and ultrasound misses many. Cardiotocographic monitoring for at least 4 to 6 hours is used once the fetus is viable.
- Uterine rupture and amniotic fluid embolism are rarer.
- Give anti-D immunoglobulin to every Rh-negative mother within 72 hours; the Kleihauer-Betke test sizes the fetomaternal bleed to set the dose.
- Necessary imaging, including CT, is not withheld.
- In cardiac arrest with the fundus at or above the umbilicus, begin resuscitative hysterotomy at 4 minutes to deliver by 5.

options.A: Too high, and not what the rule gives. The second space is a needle-decompression landmark, not a drain site.
options.B: The fifth space is the usual site in the non-pregnant adult; in late pregnancy it risks passing through or below the raised diaphragm.
options.C: Correct. One to two spaces above the usual fifth space.
options.D: Never; a tube below the diaphragm is in the abdomen.

117.picks_note: Your pick, A. You had the right direction (go higher) but went too far; the second space is remembered from needle decompression. The adjustment is one or two spaces up from the fifth, which gives the third or fourth.

118.why: One act (giving a sedative or opioid) has two effects: relief of suffering, which is intended, and a possible earlier death, which is foreseen but not intended. The doctrine of double effect is the named principle that makes such an act ethical, provided the dose is titrated to the symptom.
118.watch: Non-maleficence ('do no harm') sounds close, but on its own it would argue against a drug that might shorten life. The stem's wording, 'foreseeable possibility of hastening death', is the signature of double effect.
118.hook: Foreseen is not the same as intended: titrate to the symptom, and what you intended is what you are judged on.

options.A: Autonomy is the patient's right to accept or refuse treatment. It explains why comfort care was chosen, not why a drug with a risky side effect may be given.
options.B: Correct. One act, two effects; the good one intended, the bad one foreseen but not intended, and the dose proportionate to the symptom.
options.C: Distributive justice is about fair allocation of scarce resources (beds, ventilators, triage). Nothing in the stem concerns allocation.
options.D: Non-maleficence is the duty to avoid harm. It is a general principle and does not resolve the conflict between relieving pain and risking death; double effect is the specific tool for that conflict.

118.picks_note: You left this blank; HT guessed it right. The phrase to recognise is 'foreseeable possibility of hastening death' beside a symptom-relief intention.

120.why: Bleomycin damages the lung through oxygen free radicals, and the resulting pneumonitis typically appears during treatment or in the months after it, up to about six months from the last dose. Symptoms starting four months after a bleomycin regimen, with no other cause, fit that window.
120.watch: The other three options are all 'immediate' or 'airway' processes. Bleomycin injury is an alveolar and interstitial process (alveolitis, then fibrosis) with a restrictive pattern, not bronchospasm or airway obstruction, and not an infection.
120.hook: Bleomycin lung is a late, restrictive, oxygen-sensitive injury: months after the drug, low DLCO, and made worse by a high FiO2.
120.explain:
## Why the lung, and why oxygen matters
Bleomycin is an antitumour antibiotic used for Hodgkin lymphoma (the B of ABVD) and germ cell tumours (the B of BEP). It binds iron and, in the presence of oxygen, generates free radicals that break DNA. Most tissues inactivate it with an enzyme, bleomycin hydrolase. The lung and the skin have very little of this enzyme, so those are the two organs it injures.

In the lung the radicals damage capillary endothelium and type I alveolar cells. This produces an alveolitis, and healing by fibroblasts then lays down collagen: pneumonitis first, fibrosis later. Because the injury is oxidative, a high inspired oxygen concentration supplies more substrate for it. That is why oxygen can precipitate or worsen the disease, even years later in theatre.

## What an examiner can ask
- **Timing:** subacute, during treatment or up to about 6 months after it. Not an infusion reaction.
- **Risk factors:** cumulative dose above about 400 units, older age (risk climbs from about 40), renal impairment (the drug is renally excreted), chest radiotherapy, high FiO2, smoking.
- **Picture:** dry cough, exertional dyspnoea, fine basal crackles; bibasal subpleural reticular or ground-glass change on CT; restrictive spirometry. A falling DLCO is the earliest test abnormality.
- **Treatment:** stop bleomycin permanently, give corticosteroids, and use the lowest FiO2 that keeps saturation acceptable (commonly 88-92%).
- **Outcome:** clinical toxicity in about 10% of treated patients and about 1% die of it; once severe pneumonitis is established, mortality is quoted up to about 25%.

## About this item
It is a diagnosis of exclusion; infection, tumour progression and radiation pneumonitis must be ruled out. The question only tests that the onset is delayed.

options.A: Correct. Onset weeks to months after exposure (up to about 6 months) is characteristic, so a normal chest immediately after chemotherapy does not exclude it.
options.B: Wrong on both words: the injury is free-radical mediated and sterile, and it is not immediate.
options.C: Bleomycin injures alveoli and interstitium, giving a restrictive defect with low DLCO. Isolated airway obstruction points elsewhere.
options.D: Acute bronchospasm is an infusion-type reaction. Bleomycin lung toxicity is subacute alveolitis progressing to fibrosis.

key.note: The stem gives few clinical details; the only thing tested is that bleomycin lung toxicity is delayed.

121.why: Confusion, hallucinations and seizures within 2-96 hours of an ifosfamide infusion, with normal imaging and a metabolic pattern on EEG, is ifosfamide-induced encephalopathy. Methylene blue (50 mg IV every 4 hours) is the specific agent reported to shorten or stop it; the other three options are not treatments for any neurological toxicity.
121.watch: The three distractors are taken from neighbouring lines of the same Oh's passage on cancer-drug toxicity (anthracycline cardiomyopathy, 5-fluorouracil coronary spasm, checkpoint inhibitors). Match the drug to its own organ before reading the options.
121.hook: Ifosfamide plus a confused patient with a normal scan: stop the infusion and give methylene blue.
121.explain:
## What is happening
Ifosfamide is an alkylating agent, a close relative of cyclophosphamide, used for sarcomas, germ cell tumours and lymphoma. It is a prodrug activated in the liver. One of its by-products, chloroacetaldehyde, crosses into the brain, where it depletes glutathione and blocks the mitochondrial respiratory chain. Neurons that cannot make ATP stop working normally, and the result is a toxic-metabolic encephalopathy: nothing structural to see on CT or MRI, and diffuse slowing on EEG.

## Why methylene blue
Methylene blue can accept and donate electrons, so it bypasses the blocked step of the respiratory chain. It also inhibits the amine oxidases that generate chloroacetaldehyde. The evidence is case series rather than trials, but it is the antidote named in Oh's and the one exams expect.

## What an examiner can ask
- **Frequency and timing:** 10-30% of patients (up to 40% with high-dose regimens); onset 2-96 hours after the infusion; usually resolves within 2-3 days of stopping the drug.
- **Spectrum:** confusion and hallucinations, extrapyramidal signs, seizures, coma. Non-convulsive status must be excluded by EEG.
- **Risk factors:** low serum albumin, renal impairment, previous cisplatin, bulky pelvic disease.
- **Diagnosis:** one of exclusion, after sepsis, electrolyte disturbance, CNS disease and other drugs are ruled out.
- **Treatment:** stop ifosfamide; methylene blue 50 mg IV 4-hourly (6-hourly has been tried as prophylaxis in later cycles, with inconsistent results); benzodiazepines for seizures; thiamine is also reported.
- **Methylene blue cautions:** it inhibits monoamine oxidase A, so it can cause serotonin syndrome with SSRIs, and it causes haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
- **Ifosfamide's other toxicities:** haemorrhagic cystitis from acrolein (prevented by mesna and hydration) and proximal tubular damage (Fanconi syndrome). Mesna does not prevent the encephalopathy.

options.A: Correct. The specific therapy for ifosfamide encephalopathy; it bypasses the mitochondrial block caused by chloroacetaldehyde.
options.B: Cardiac resynchronisation is a device therapy for heart failure with a wide QRS, mentioned in the source for anthracycline cardiomyopathy.
options.C: Coronary vasodilators (nitrates, calcium channel blockers) treat the coronary vasospasm of 5-fluorouracil and capecitabine.
options.D: Checkpoint inhibitors (anti-PD-1, anti-CTLA-4) are cancer treatments that themselves cause immune toxicities; they treat nothing here.

121.picks_note: You guessed A correctly. HT picked D, immune checkpoint blockade: that is a class of anticancer drugs, not a rescue therapy, and it appears only because the same passage discusses it.

key.note: The stem says 'supported by the supplied passage', so the key follows Oh's text. Methylene blue is also the accepted answer in general, although the evidence for it is case-series level.

122.why: Blocking the superior vena cava raises venous pressure in everything it drains: face, arms, upper airway and brain. Swelling of the face and arms is uncomfortable but harmless. Swelling of the brain (headache, then drowsiness) and of the larynx (stridor) can kill, and of those two only cerebral oedema is offered.
122.watch: Facial and arm swelling are the commonest findings, which is why they are tempting, but they mark the diagnosis, not the danger. The stem's new features are drowsiness and stridor; the answer has to explain one of them.
122.hook: In SVC obstruction the swelling you can see makes the diagnosis; the swelling you cannot see (brain, larynx) makes it an emergency.
122.explain:
## Why obstruction causes this picture
The superior vena cava is a thin-walled, low-pressure vein lying in a tight space between the trachea, the right main bronchus, the aorta and chains of lymph nodes. A mass in the mediastinum compresses it easily; a clot around a central line or pacing lead can block it from inside. Venous pressure upstream rises and fluid leaks into the tissues of the head, neck and arms.

Speed decides severity. When obstruction develops over weeks, blood finds other routes to the heart through the azygos, internal mammary, lateral thoracic and oesophageal veins, and symptoms are mild. When it develops quickly, or when the block lies at or below the entry of the azygos vein so that the main bypass is lost, pressure rises sharply.
